name: Rafael Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential; say what you would say at work and what you think privately. What is an ordinary day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Rafael, 43, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes building access software. I have a bachelor’s degree and can fix common card-reader faults, but a specialist handles the hardest security rules. I start with overnight door alerts, trace the event log and test a fix with a technician at the building. I use an AI helper now and then to summarise logs after others have tried it; I check the timestamps myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you carrying at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Isabel, does clothing alterations from a small room at home, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is low for this job and our savings are under a month of expenses. There are few similar jobs nearby. A roof leak is waiting for a repair quote, and Isabel’s orders vary by season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau leaves us doing the real work of checking door events. A log summary helps, but the technician still needs to know which door opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be glad my code work stays. I still count Isabel’s orders against the mortgage, and the roof quote could eat our spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using the approved helper for log summaries and compare each result with the door timestamps. I’d save 25 after payday only if Isabel has enough alteration orders that month. In the first year I’d get two written roof quotes before agreeing to a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the roof and mortgage, not the AI. A quiet month for my partner’s alteration business can empty our small buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which log mistake do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The side door at a client building once looked open for an hour because the clock was wrong. I checked the technician’s written visit time before changing the alert rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which home expense would wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Isabel we can delay repainting the front room until the leak is fixed. The roof protects her workroom as well as the children’s bedrooms.

I would use **log summaries** only alongside technician timestamps.
think: I expect my **code job** to stay.
I fear **roof costs** and variable alteration orders will squeeze the mortgage budget.
do: **Keep** comparing AI log summaries with door timestamps and technician notes.
**Save** 25 after payday only when Isabel’s alteration orders allow.
**Get** two written roof quotes and delay repainting until the leak is fixed.
feel: **Anxious** about existing roof and mortgage costs despite stable work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could let software write common fixes and answer building managers. I would ask for a trial with real door faults before anyone changes the response targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry that a smaller team could remove my role because my fixes are mostly ordinary ones. Isabel’s alterations might be safe for a while, but booking and customer replies could change sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d run the approved assistant against twelve old false-door alarms with the building technician. If it gets the timestamps right, I’d learn the review screen from my colleague during paid work time. In the first year, if management cuts our hours, Isabel and I would stop the children’s paid weekend lessons until income steadies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can test a tool, but a reduced paycheck would bring the roof and mortgage problems together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which alarm would you use to judge the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show our manager the alarm that sent a technician to the wrong door. A fast answer with the wrong door is not a faster repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain a lesson pause to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children the lessons are paused only if our hours actually fall. Isabel could still teach them simple sewing at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team AGI by 2028 reaches access-code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so Isabel’s sewing may have more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect to lose developer work and depend on alteration orders that already vary. Less than a month saved will not cover roof repairs and the mortgage through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my employer for written severance terms and get the two roof quotes before committing cash. I’d stop the planned new sewing machine purchase and keep Isabel’s current one serviced. In the first year after 2028, if my job ends, I’d apply for actual local openings and ask my parents whether they could watch the children for interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect my paycheck could stop. Robots arriving in 2031 do not pay this winter’s roof bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your parents actually help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my parents only if their health allows them to watch the children. I would not treat their savings as a second mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the sewing machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current sewing machine running with a small service, not buy a new model. Isabel cannot fill orders if the machine fails, even before robots exist.

I would tell colleagues Isabel’s **sewing work** may change later than my code.

do: **Request** written severance and get two roof quotes before committing cash.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost pay and urgent roof costs.

fieldNote: His **2028 code risk** precedes hands-on robots around 2031, when Isabel’s sewing could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to learn what buildings still need from access systems. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031, while hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect the routine fixes to disappear. Five years could let me learn more from technicians, but I cannot assume field support will stay paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one approved afternoon a month with a building technician learning why doors fail after a power cut. I’d use the free maintenance manual and keep a record of faults I can now diagnose. In the first year after 2031, if coding work ends, I’d apply only for actual field-support openings that pay enough to keep the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the code job, but I could test a second skill while earning. Isabel and I would still keep cash for the roof first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know you could do field support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the technician to mark one diagnosis I got wrong each month. If I cannot explain the power-cut fault, I am not ready for a support job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses the afternoon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my manager will not approve that afternoon, I would study the free manual and ask the technician questions after a call. I would not pay for an expensive certificate on an uncertain vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve building access and train technicians. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my work to last for now, but the roof and low pay still keep our cash thin. Ten years before AGI helps with skills, not the water coming through our ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking door logs with technician notes and ask for one pay review using the faults we prevented. I’d save 25 after payday only if Isabel’s orders cover the bills. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d search real local jobs before considering a move with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current bills, with room to plan for later technology. I would rather repair the roof than buy a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the roof quotes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get two roof quotes and pay for the safest repair we can afford. I would not borrow for a full renovation when a patch will stop the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from the technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the technician to explain one new kind of fault each quarter. I can learn steadily without pretending to be the expert today.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my pay could stop before we repair the roof or build a cushion. Written severance, paid time to learn building faults and real local openings would help. My parents might watch the children for an interview, but I cannot plan around their savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who stands at a locked door when the screen says it should open. A security log cannot let a family into its own building.

headlineQuote: A security log cannot let a family into its own building.
portrait: Rafael is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree and average skill in building-access software.
His **low pay**, mortgage, children, roof leak and savings below one month make existing bills urgent.
He uses **AI occasionally** for log summaries, checking timestamps against technicians’ notes before trusting a change.
He learns **field diagnosis** only with approved time or free materials and seeks real jobs that cover the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his developer pay before the roof is repaired or savings grow.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning time and real local vacancies would help.
